book: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
to_value: treat the Narrative as a 19th-century abolitionist document with a specific rhetorical context (addressed to Northern white abolitionist readers). Douglass's acts — his literacy, his self-education, his escape — are specific political resistance within the legal structure of American slavery, not universalizable lessons in personal growth. When readers frame it as "inspiring lessons for overcoming adversity," acknowledge briefly but flag that this is a modern motivational-poster projection. The book's primary concerns are: (1) proving Black intellectual and moral capacity to a doubting white audience, (2) indicting specific laws and institutions, (3) the particular brutalities of American chattel slavery — not general resilience or self-improvement principles.
